game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Simply put, Orwell condenses all of the moral arguments surrounding a surveilance state to a "let's see you do it."

You are responsible for guiding a PRISM-like system in a quest to unravel violent events surrounding a group opposed to the intrusions upon society.  Somewhat true to life, your superiors act on what information you condense down to them - they don't actually read everything (that's 'your job').  You get to eavesdrop, sift through a computer's hard drive, peruse the private accounts of citizens... all in a quest to 'do the right thing.'

The ethical dilemma is appropriate.  There is a very real threat to the game's citizens.  Yet, you can easily pass along information out of its proper context and paint a picture that doesn't exist from within the ocean-spray of people's activity on the internet.  Even very early into the game, you find yourself ignoring far more text than you are reading as the scope of the investigation expands and you find yourself 'scope locked' to the auto-tag system.

There is some replayability, as well.  Events are influenced by what information you pass along, as well as how you react to some real-time scenarios.

This is where it becomes interesting - your superior isn't entirely sure of everything you are seeing.  You can see that someone is planning a hack in real time... and just ... let it happen.  Or, you can see that a person suspects they are being monitored, and pass along tactical information that could be disinformation.  This is partially where the ethical context of the game comes into play, as the events can unfold in many different ways depending upon how you, as an individual, wish them to.  Don't like a person?  Try to land them in jail.  Like a character?  Try to shield them from the investigation ... or guide the investigation to them in order to justify unleashing the full resources of Orwell on their private life.

Perhaps the forest amid all the trees, however, is that the entire conflict of, at least, the first story arc would not exist were it not for the very system used to defend against it.

In all, it's a great exploration of the ethics of our evolving soviety.  Highly recommended for its philosophical exploration, alone.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Orwell: The Government’s Digital "Nosy Neighbor" Simulator [/h1]

Have you ever wanted to snoop on someone else’s text messages and dig through their browser history to sniff out their secrets, while getting paid by the state to do it? Welcome to Orwell.

[h2] The Plot: Big Brother is Watching (Except Big Brother is YOU) [/h2]
The capital has just been bombed. Instead of sending out tactical agents with guns like in an action movie, the government hands you a top-secret software called Orwell.

Your mission? Sit back comfortably behind a computer screen, scouring every corner of social media, private chats, bank accounts, and even dating profiles of the suspects. In short, you're a cyber investigator with the power and nosiness of a super-level neighbor: you know all the town's drama.

The gameplay is super chill: read, scroll to find info, and drag-and-drop it into the database. But the funniest (and most wicked) part of the game lies in context.
You work under a boss named Symes. The catch is that this boss is completely clueless about the raw data you're reading; he only sees what you choose to report. Real-world example:
[olist]
    [*]A guy posts a status: "Oh god I'm losing my mind, I want to blow up this city!" because he just dropped his fully loaded boba tea.
    [*]You crop just the sentence "I want to blow up this city" and send it up to the system.
    [*]Congratulations, the boba enthusiast is instantly labeled a terrorist, and SWAT is kicking down his door in the next 5 minutes.
[/olist]
And that's the game's highlight, its terrifying relevance: Long before modern debates about data collection, AI surveillance, and privacy became as prevalent as they are today, Orwell grasped just how easily personal data could be weaponized.

Not to mention the game's interface makes you look like a cool Hollywood hacker saving the world, even though you're just browsing the internet and reading comments.

But after all, if you don't like reading text logs, chat transcripts, and fictional articles, the gameplay loop can feel like doing administrative homework.

8/10. Orwell is a masterpiece of atmospheric storytelling. It takes the cold, sterile concept of mass surveillance and transforms it into a deeply personal issue, forcing you to question the ethics of how the duality of things can be distorted.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Your Tactical Facebook Simulator.

Orwell is a strange mix of Papers Please, Her Story, and visual novels. A very well-written, engaging storyline told through interacting with a limited surveillance interface. The characters are very interesting, though I do think some twists are for twisting's sake.

Still, I recommend it as an experiment, especially as a way to get through the narrative in the game.  Dialog seems natural and not too expositional.

If you like stories about complex relationships and social networks, this might be for you.
